pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 2–3). Skip counting in 4s, 8s, 50s and 100s — extending equal-step counting into the multiplication-facts that underpin the times tables.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.2 'skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; 3.OA.7 recall of products (the 4s and 8s underpin the ×4 and ×8 tables); 3.NBT.3 multiply one-digit by multiples of 10.
• Operational details: teach 4s and 8s through the DOUBLING CHAIN — 2s doubled give 4s, 4s doubled give 8s (each 8-step is two 4-steps is four 2-steps). 50s are half-hundreds/money (two 50s make 100) and 100s extend the place-value step. Counting in 4s and 8s is explicitly the equal-groups on-ramp to the 4 and 8 times tables.
• Checkpoint: skip-count fluently and connect to equal groups. Tier A (7): count in 4s and 100s from 0 with a number-line/hundred-square prop. Tier B (7–8): count in 4s, 8s, 50s, 100s from 0 and state the matching equal-groups fact (three 4s = 12). Tier C (8): explain 8s as doubled 4s and 4s as doubled 2s, and count 50s to 500 linking two 50s = 100.
bestPractices: Build 4s and 8s from the DOUBLING relationship rather than as separate chants: stack a 2s number line, a 4s line and an 8s line so the child sees each 4-jump spans two 2-jumps and each 8-jump spans two 4-jumps.

Tie every skip count to equal groups and the array — counting 4, 8, 12, 16 is one group, two groups, three groups of four — so skip counting is experienced as repeated addition and the direct route into the ×4 and ×8 tables.
Anchor 50s in money and half-hundreds: two 50p coins make £1, two 50s make 100, so counting 50, 100, 150 is felt as pairing up to hundreds rather than a new memorised list.
Use the hundred square to expose the visual pattern of each count (the 4s and 8s make regular diagonal/column patterns; 50s and 100s march down rows) so the pattern is seen, not just heard.

Rehearse forwards and backwards and from non-zero starts once the forward count is secure, and connect back to previously mastered 2s/5s/10s so the new counts join a coherent web rather than standing alone.
keyRepresentations: Stacked/aligned number lines (2s, 4s, 8s) showing the doubling of jump size
Equal groups and arrays (groups of 4, groups of 8) linking the count to repeated addition and multiplication
Hundred square with each multiple shaded to reveal the pattern (4s, 8s columns/diagonals; 50s and 100s down the rows)
Coins and a money line (50p, £1) anchoring the 50s count in half-hundreds
commonMisconceptions: Treating 4s and 8s as unrelated rote lists and never noticing 8s are doubled 4s — so a slip in one count cannot be repaired from the other.
Adding the wrong step (drifting into 2s when counting 4s, or 5s when counting 50s) because the step size isn't held steady.
Miscounting 50s as 'fifties are like fives with a zero' and producing 50, 100, 150, 250 — losing a step or mis-pairing to hundreds.
Not connecting the skip count to groups, so the child can chant 4, 8, 12 but cannot say how many groups of four make 12 — the count stays verbal and never becomes multiplicative.
Boundary slips crossing hundreds while counting in 50s or 100s (150→200, 950→1000) when the hundreds digit must roll.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 2–3): counting from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100, built on the doubling chain (2s doubled are 4s, 4s doubled are 8s) and tied explicitly to equal groups so skip counting becomes the on-ramp to the ×4 and ×8 tables. 50s are anchored in money/half-hundreds (two 50s make 100). The central insight to teach is the relationship between step sizes — that each 8-jump spans two 4-jumps spans four 2-jumps — and the connection between a verbal count and 'how many groups'.

activities.title: The doubling chain: stacked number lines for 2s, 4s and 8s
feedback: If a learner sub-counts (audibly counting 4-by-4 or one-by-one to reach the next 8), do not drill for speed. Point to the known 4s fact and prompt 'double it' — fluency grows through repeated jumps on the number line, not pressure.
If a learner treats 4s and 8s as unrelated, write out the 4s from 0 and ring every second number (0, 8, 16…) to reveal the 8s: 'the 8s take a jump twice as big.'
When a learner lands correctly, ask them to show which smaller jumps live inside the big jump, so the doubling is explained, not just recited.
activities.rationale: The target relationship is between step sizes, which becomes visible when the counts are laid against each other and the jumps aligned. Building 4s and 8s from doubling rather than as separate chants gives learners a repair strategy and links directly to the ×4 and ×8 tables. Optional interactive versions (buttons that advance each line, with smaller jumps ghosting in beneath each larger step) may make the nesting more manipulable; a paper version with three aligned strips achieves the same alignment.
sourceClaims: Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Lay out (or display) three aligned number lines starting at 0: one marked in 2s, one in 4s, one in 8s, with the same spacing so matching numbers sit directly above one another.
Step along the 8s line one jump at a time. For each 8-jump, mark the two 4-jumps directly beneath it, and the four 2-jumps beneath those.
Say aloud as you go: 'one jump of 8 is the same distance as two jumps of 4, which is four jumps of 2.'
Count the 4s aloud (0, 4, 8, 12, 16…) and ring every other number starting from 0 — notice the circled numbers are exactly the 8s count (0, 8, 16…).
Count backwards in 8s from 96, checking each step against the 4s line.
Repeat from a non-zero start once the forward count is secure (e.g. count on in 4s from 24).
Link the new counts back to the 2s, 5s and 10s you already know, so 4s/8s/50s/100s join a coherent web rather than standing alone.
activities.intendedInsight: 8s are doubled 4s and 4s are doubled 2s; a slip in one count can be repaired using the other, because the step sizes nest inside each other.

activities.title: From skip count to equal groups and arrays
feedback: If a learner can chant '4, 8, 12' but cannot say how many groups of four make 12, rebuild with physical groups so each number names one more group.
If a learner answers 'how many fours in 20' by guessing, have them step the number line and tally the jumps.
Confirm success when the learner moves fluently between the count, the groups and the product.
activities.rationale: Tying every skip count to equal groups and the array makes the count multiplicative rather than purely verbal, and matching items test the count-to-groups connection directly. This is the bridge from counting to table recall.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2 skip-count by 5s, 10s and 100s; 3.OA.7 fluently multiply and recall products — counting in 4s and 8s underpins the ×4 and ×8 tables.
Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Build groups of four with counters: one group, two groups, three groups, saying the running total (4, 8, 12) and the matching fact ('three fours = 12').
Arrange the same counters into an array (rows of four) so each skip-count step adds one row.
Match skip-count totals to equal-groups statements, e.g. pair 'three groups of 8' with 24, 'five fours' with 20.
Answer group-count challenges in both directions: 'How many fours in 20?' (five) and 'What is four groups of eight?' (32).
Repeat the build for groups of eight, noticing each group of eight is two groups of four.
activities.intendedInsight: A skip count is repeated addition of equal groups; knowing the count lets you say how many groups make a total, which is exactly the multiplication fact.

activities.title: Counting in 50s and 100s with money and the hundred square
feedback: If a learner says 50, 100, 150, 250 (losing a step), do not reteach the whole sequence — rehearse the specific boundary bridge (…, 150, 200) with coins or a number line.
If a learner loses place crossing a hundred, slow down at the boundary and name the rolling hundreds digit aloud.

If a learner uses '50s are like 5s with a zero', accept it as a valid pattern (each 50s number is ten times the matching 5s number), and also build meaning by pairing coins to hundreds so they can explain why 150 + 50 = 200.
activities.rationale: Anchoring 50s in money and half-hundreds makes the count felt as pairing to hundreds rather than a new memorised list, and the hundred square and number line expose the visual pattern so it is seen, not only heard. Targeting boundary crossings addresses a common place-value slip. No cited source directly supports this money-anchoring approach, so it is offered as a research-informed proposal.
learnerActions: Pair up 50p coins (or £50 notes) to make pounds/hundreds: two 50s make 100, so count 50, 100, 150, 200… pairing as you go.
Count on in 50s from 0 to 1000, deliberately slowing at each hundred boundary (…, 450, 500, 550; …, 950, 1000) and checking the hundreds digit rolls correctly.

On a 1–100 hundred square, shade the 4s and 8s to see their column/diagonal patterns; then on a number line or track to 1000, mark the 50s and 100s to see them step evenly, with 50s landing twice as often as 100s.
Count in 100s from 0 to 1000 and compare with the 50s on the same number line.
State explicitly: 'how many 50s make 1000?' and check by pairing (two 50s = 100, so twenty 50s = 1000).
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in 50s can be understood as pairing up to hundreds (two 50s make 100); it also matches the 5s count with each number ten times bigger (5, 10, 15 → 50, 100, 150), but the pairing view carries the meaning. Boundary crossings require the hundreds digit to roll, and shading/marking makes each count's pattern visible.

activities.title: Oral fluency and self-check with a counting partner
feedback: If totals disagree between the 8s and 'two lots of 4s' check, find the step where they diverge and re-jump it.
Praise self-correction that uses the 4s to repair the 8s rather than restarting.
activities.rationale: Spoken rehearsal with responsive prompting may support oral fluency and keeps the doubling link active; it is intended to complement the visual/structural work rather than replace it, and is best used once the structure is understood rather than as the first route in. Its effectiveness relative to the manipulative is untested.
sourceClaims: Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Count in 8s aloud with a partner, taking turns on each step.
Check an 8s count against the 4s count, confirming that each 8s step equals two 4s steps (e.g. two jumps of 4 reach 8, four jumps of 4 reach 16).
Have the partner pose doubling prompts: 'If four fours are 16, what are four eights?'
Count forwards and backwards from non-zero starts to build flexibility, and relate the counts to the already-known 2s, 5s and 10s.
activities.intendedInsight: Oral rehearsal and self-checking against a related count build fluency and reinforce that the 4s and 8s support each other.

constraints: Counting in 4s and 8s is best built from the doubling relationship, not taught as separate rote chants, so learners can repair one count from the other.
Every skip count should be tied to equal groups/arrays so the count becomes multiplicative, not merely verbal.
Do not drill for speed when a learner is sub-counting; connect to the known related count and let fluency grow through repeated jumps and retrieval.

Sequence, fill-in-the-blank and matching exercises can check these counts but do not by themselves build the doubling structure — use them to check mastery after the relationship has been taught; a sort/match verifies classification without eliciting an explanation of why 8s are doubled 4s.

A pre-shaded pattern reference (static or tap-to-reveal) supports pattern spotting and the equal-groups link but does not let the learner drive the count or see the doubling animate; treat it as a reference, not the primary build.

Interactive overlays (advancing lines, ghosted smaller jumps, live shading) and physical coins are optional concrete aids to make the mechanism visible; they are means, not required mechanisms — aligned paper strips and real coins work too.
A standard 1–100 hundred square displays the 4s/8s patterns; use a number line or track for 50s and 100s up to 1000.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the counts: 4s from 0 to 48 (0,4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32,36,40,44,48), 8s from 0 to 96 (0,8,…,96), and 50s to 1000 (twenty steps of 50) are all arithmetically consistent. 'Every second multiple of 4, counting from 0, is a multiple of 8' is correct (0,8,16… are the even-indexed 4s). Equal-groups facts used are correct: three fours = 12, five fours = 20, three eights = 24, four eights = 32, twenty fifties = 1000.
The source's erroneous example sequence '50, 100, 150, 250' (used to illustrate a learner error) is preserved only as a misconception to correct, never presented as a valid count.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (the CCSS-M and NCETM claims); treat their specific wordings as unconfirmed, and the doubling/equal-groups pedagogy as a recommended rather than empirically proven approach.

Activity 3 (50s/100s money and boundary work) has sourceClaims set to [] because none of the cited claims directly supports its money-anchoring/boundary-roll teaching principle; it is a research-informed proposal only.

The original research rated a 3D environment as adding 'no conceptual gain' for these planar patterns. That is a catalog fit judgement, not a pedagogical law; flat aligned views are proposed because the doubling overlay and hundred-square pattern read clearly in 2D, without claiming 3D cannot teach it.

The original keyRepresentation referred to a 'hundred square' for 50s/100s; a 1–100 square cannot show these to 1000, so a number line/track is used instead for those counts. The 4s/8s remain on the hundred square.

probeDeeper: What's the next multiple of 8 after 56?
How is counting in 8s like counting in 4s?
What's 4 more than 44? And 8 more than 88?
assess.correctAnswer: 0, 4, 8, …, 48; 0, 8, 16, …, 96; 0, 50, 100, …, 1000; and notices 8s are the 4s doubled (every second multiple of 4) — each step adds the group size.

errorPatterns.pattern: sub-counts by smaller steps — builds the 8s by counting on in 4s (or ones) each time rather than stepping by 8; slow and breaks under load
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill for speed — use number-line jumps of 8 and connect to the known 4s ('double it'); fluency grows with practice and retrieval
errorPatterns.revealedBy: audible intermediate counting between the multiples of 8

errorPatterns.pattern: no link between 4s and 8s — treats them as two separate lists, doesn't see 8s as doubled 4s
errorPatterns.nextMove: write out the 4s and ring every other one to reveal the 8s — 'a jump twice as big' — making the doubling relationship explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the sequences are unrelated, or can't use the 4s to get the 8s

errorPatterns.pattern: 50s/100s digit slip — loses place in the 50s (…, 450, 500, 550) or miscounts at boundaries
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT reteach the whole sequence — pair 50s with money (£50 notes) or a number line and rehearse the …950, 1000 bridge specifically

responseLevels.gap: Cannot sustain 4s/8s beyond a few terms without counting every one, and treats each sequence as unrelated.
responseLevels.full: Skip-counts 4s, 8s, 50s, 100s fluently, steps by the group size without sub-counting, and uses the 4s-doubled-are-8s relationship.
responseLevels.partial: Recites 4s, 8s, 50s from 0 but sub-counts for each step, or cannot exploit the 4s↔8s doubling link.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count in 4s from 0 to 48. Now count in 8s from 0 to 96. Then count in 50s to 1000. And as you do the 8s, tell me — how could counting in 4s help you count in 8s? (Watch fluency, sub-counting, and whether they see 8s as double the 4s.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 4s and 8s have weaker rhythmic support than 2s/5s/10s, so this exposes children who chant only well-patterned sequences. The 'how do 4s help 8s' question tests whether the child sees the doubling relationship — a bridge to the 4× and 8× tables — rather than treating the sequences as unrelated. Sub-counting by ones/fours, or no link between 4s and 8s, marks a fragile grasp.
